title: Could You Survive a Volcanic Eruption Up Close?

scenes.text: A cloud hotter than an oven is rolling toward you at up to seven hundred kilometers an hour. But the lava everyone fears is the least dangerous thing here. So what actually kills you?

scenes.question: How close is too close?
scenes.heading: Mount St. Helens, 1980
scenes.text: This is Mount St. Helens in Washington State, on the morning of May eighteenth, nineteen eighty. We will use its eruption as our map, and walk toward the crater distance by distance: ten kilometers, five, one, a hundred meters, and finally the vent. Watch what each step does to your body.

label: 10 KM
Ashfall zone
scenes.fact: Volcanic ash is tiny jagged glass and rock,\Nnot soft like fireplace ash.
scenes.text: Ten kilometers out, the sky turns gray. Ash is not soft like fireplace dust. It is tiny, jagged fragments of glass and rock. Wet ash piles up heavy enough to collapse a roof. Breathe it unprotected and it scratches your lungs and eyes. A mask or damp cloth helps a lot.

chapter: WHAT'S IN THE AIR AT 5 KM?
label: 5 KM
Gas zone
scenes.text: Five kilometers. Now the danger is invisible. Volcanoes breathe out steam, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Sulfur dioxide burns your eyes, throat and lungs. Carbon dioxide has no smell, and it is heavier than air, so it pools in low ground. Stay upwind, and stay out of hollows.

scenes.question: How hot is lava as it leaves the volcano?
scenes.text: Quick question, before we go closer. How hot is lava when it leaves the ground?

label: 3 KM
The sideways blast
scenes.text: At eight thirty-two that morning, an earthquake shakes the mountain and its north face slides away. The largest landslide in recorded history uncorks the magma inside. The blast does not go up. It goes sideways.

scenes.heading: MAY 18, 1980
scenes.text: Ten kilometers away should have been safe. It was not. The blast raced across the land at hundreds of kilometers an hour, flattening forest as far as about twenty-five kilometers away. Volcanologist David Johnston was watching from about ten kilometers. His last radio call: Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it! Fifty-seven people died that day. Johnston was one of them.

scenes.question: What is a pyroclastic flow?
scenes.heading: What one leaves behind
scenes.text: You cannot outrun this. Nothing alive can. A pyroclastic flow is an avalanche of hot gas, ash and rock that pours down the volcano's slopes, hugging the ground and following valleys, dense enough to flatten buildings yet fluid enough to pour like water. It can reach about seven hundred kilometers an hour. This is what one leaves behind in a valley.

scenes.caption: FASTEST PYROCLASTIC FLOWS
scenes.text: Several hundred degrees Celsius. A kitchen oven tops out near two hundred and fifty. Nothing you wear changes that.

scenes.heading: YOU VS THE FLOW
scenes.text: You, at a flat-out sprint, manage well under forty. You cannot outrun it. The only protection is distance, or never being in its valley.

label: AD 79
Pompeii
scenes.text: In the year seventy-nine, Vesuvius erupts. For hours, pumice and ash rain on Pompeii, and many flee. Then, early the next morning, pyroclastic surges sweep through the city. Studies suggest the heat alone could kill within seconds to minutes. Those who stayed were buried.

scenes.label: A CAST FROM POMPEII
scenes.text: Centuries later, archaeologists found hollows in the hardened ash where bodies had been. Filling them with plaster gave us these casts. They are not statues. They are the shape of the last moment.

label: 100 M
Lava zone
scenes.fact: Pahoehoe lava often creeps slower than\Na walking pace.
scenes.text: The thing you fear most at a volcano is the least dangerous. A hundred meters from the lava. It is around eleven hundred degrees Celsius, hot enough to glow orange, and the heat on your face is fierce. But look how slowly it moves. On Kilauea, lava often creeps at less than walking pace. You can simply step away. Lava destroys houses. It rarely catches people.

label: THE VENT
Ground zero
scenes.text: At the vent, the danger is not the lava. It is what flies out of it. Explosions throw rocks out of the crater faster than a car on a highway. In twenty fourteen, at Mount Ontake in Japan, a sudden eruption killed dozens of hikers, mostly with flying rocks.
If you survive the rocks, you meet the fountains. Lava thrown tens of meters into the air, bright as noon at night. Beautiful, from far away. From up close, one of the most dangerous places on Earth.

scenes.question: What comes hours later?
scenes.heading: A lahar
scenes.text: Now step back, far back. Fifty kilometers from the vent, there is one more killer, and it arrives hours later. A lahar. Ash mixes with rain, melted snow or ice, and becomes a flood of wet concrete racing down river valleys. In nineteen eighty-five, lahars from Nevado del Ruiz buried the town of Armero in Colombia, killing more than twenty thousand people.

scenes.heading: WHAT ACTUALLY KILLS
scenes.text: So, could you survive an eruption up close? Not at the vent, and not in the path of a pyroclastic flow. Lava is the least of your problems. What saves people is distance, obeying evacuation orders, a mask against ash, and climbing away from valleys when a lahar threatens.
Distance. A mask. High ground. That is the whole survival guide.
If you liked the walk toward the volcano, subscribe to Oddly Logical Science. Every week, the strangest true science. And tell me in the comments how close you would have dared to get.

youtube.title: Could You Survive a Volcanic Eruption Up Close?
youtube.description:
Could you survive a volcanic eruption up close? We walk toward an erupting volcano, distance by distance, using Mount St. Helens in 1980 as our map: ash at 10 km, gases at 5 km, the sideways blast, the pyroclastic flow that can reach about 700 km/h, the Pompeii casts, lava at around 1,100 degrees Celsius, and the lahars that arrive hours later. The surprise: lava is the least dangerous thing here.

In this video:
- What happens at 10 km?
- What's in the air at 5 km?
- The blast that went sideways
- What is a pyroclastic flow?
- What happened at Pompeii?
- Is lava the killer?
- What's at the vent?
- What is a lahar?

FAQ
How fast is a pyroclastic flow? Up to about 700 km/h, with temperatures of several hundred degrees Celsius.
Can you outrun lava? Usually yes: pahoehoe lava often moves slower than walking pace.
What kills most people in an eruption? Pyroclastic flows, blasts, flying rocks and lahars, more than lava itself.
How many people died at Mount St. Helens in 1980? 57.
How do you survive a lahar? Move uphill, out of the river valley.
